title: The One With The Home Study

jokes.text: I came up with a couple of cost-cutting solutions, wrote out a list and Monica told me to go to hell.
jokes.setup: Chandler sets up that he found a 'pretty simple' solution to wedding costs, implying a reasonable plan.
jokes.punchline: Monica's response was to tell him to go to hell — the simplicity is entirely one-sided.
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler/Monica dynamic delivered economically. The misdirection of 'pretty simple actually' building to Monica's rejection is well-structured and deeply character-specific — only Chandler would frame a dismissal this way. Gets a solid laugh in the cold open.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I've been thinking about the wedding costs, and I have a solution. What if we cut the guest list in half?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What if we have it in a park instead of a venue?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, what if we just elope?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, Chandler.

jokes.text: I heard weddings are like a 40-billion-dollar-a-year industry. Yeah, and I'm responsible for just like half of that.
jokes.setup: Ross states a large industry statistic about wedding costs.
jokes.punchline: Monica claims she's responsible for half the industry's revenue, implying her extravagance.
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific joke reinforcing Monica's compulsive over-spending on weddings. The hyperbole is funny but not particularly original — the 'I'm responsible for X industry' format is familiar. Works because it's perfectly calibrated to Monica's established character.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, I have to take responsibility for at least half of that.

jokes.text: Maybe you do that next time you get married.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica compliment Phoebe and Mike for donating their wedding money to charity.
jokes.punchline: Chandler casually references the fact that Monica has been married before, suggesting she'll have another chance to be charitable.
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. Chandler weaponizes Monica's prior marriage as a throwaway compliment that doubles as a dig. The casualness makes it land harder. Monica's immediate self-correcting follow-up ('the next time's going to be Hawaii') adds a perfect button. Good economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We decided to donate all our wedding gifts to charity.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's so generous! You guys are amazing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, really beautiful. So, uh, when's the divorce?

jokes.text: No, no, no, the next time's going to be Hawaii at sunset. But maybe the time after that.
jokes.setup: Chandler suggests Monica could donate her next wedding money to charity. Monica immediately corrects him.
jokes.punchline: Monica has already planned out multiple future weddings, the charitable one being at least two marriages away.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. The escalation from one future wedding to multiple planned future weddings is very character-specific for Monica. The rewatch bonus applies because you catch the full implication that she's pre-planned at least two additional weddings.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm not worried. I'm just gonna marry him, then in like five years we'll get divorced, and then I'll marry someone else.

jokes.text: 'We'? You know you don't want me to help. You can't have it both ways!
jokes.setup: Monica says 'we're cleaning the apartment' for the adoption social worker.
jokes.punchline: Chandler pointedly questions the 'we,' implying Monica always excludes him from cleaning. Monica's defensive response confirms it.
jokes.explanation: Familiar Monica-as-control-freak territory. The two-beat exchange works efficiently and is true to character, but it's well-trodden ground for this couple by Season 10.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm already planning my second marriage in Hawaii. Now I'm considering a third marriage for charity.

jokes.text: Hey, maybe I should stop by. She could be a soap opera fan. It's very impressive when the little people know a celebrity.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler explain the adoption social worker could affect their entire future.
jokes.punchline: Joey volunteers himself as a celebrity asset, referring to non-celebrities as 'little people' — completely misreading the gravity of the situation with supreme narcissism.
jokes.explanation: Very Joey — the obliviousness combined with self-aggrandizement is perfectly calibrated. 'Little people' is a funny word choice that doubles down on his detachment from reality. Sets up the entire Joey-and-the-social-worker subplot beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're cleaning the apartment? Since when do I clean? I'm not even sure I know how to hold a sponge.

jokes.text: "Little people"? / "Celebrity"!
jokes.setup: Joey suggests he come by because 'it's very impressive when the little people know a celebrity.'
jokes.punchline: Monica and Chandler each seize on a different offensive part of his statement simultaneously, perfectly expressing the two layers of absurdity.
jokes.explanation: A precision two-part reaction that dissects both absurdities in Joey's statement simultaneously. The split reaction is a classic multi-cam technique executed cleanly here.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We need to clean the apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We? You just told me to go to the store!

jokes.text: So there's not a magazine under the couch or a pack of cigarettes taped to the back of the toilet tank, or a filthy video in the VCR?
jokes.setup: Monica asks Chandler if he has anything bad hidden in the apartment ahead of the social worker's visit.
jokes.punchline: She lists three increasingly specific hiding spots, revealing she already knows exactly where everything is.
jokes.explanation: The escalating specificity of the hiding spots is the joke — Monica clearly knows about all of this already, making Chandler's initial denial absurd. The rule-of-three structure works well and the specificity (taped to the back of the tank, specifically) earns a laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, I got this. I've done a lot of acting, so I know how to convince people of things that aren't true.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You just gotta make them think you're something you're not. Like, you're not celebrities, but we can work around that.

jokes.text: I admit to the cigarettes and the magazine, but that tape is not mine. Well, it isn't mine! I guess we'll never know whose it is.
jokes.setup: Chandler denies the VCR tape. Monica also denies it.
jokes.punchline: Both deny the tape, so it's a mystery — the reveal that an unidentified dirty tape exists in their home with no owner claimed.
jokes.explanation: The mutual denial is funny on its own, but 'I guess we'll never know' delivered with a shrug is a perfect button — implying both are either lying or genuinely don't know, neither of which is reassuring. Good deadpan understatement from Monica.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Did you just call me stupid?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no. I called you *naive*.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's not better!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know, but at least you'll understand what it means.

jokes.text: And we don't want any recognition. This is completely anonymous. Completely anonymous. From two kind strangers. Mr. X and Phoebe Buffay.
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Mike announce they want to give anonymously to charity.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately gives her full real name while calling them 'anonymous strangers.'
jokes.explanation: Very Phoebe — she sincerely wants to be anonymous but can't help herself. The layering (Mr. X, then Phoebe Buffay, then Mike correcting as 'Mike Hannigan') creates a nice triple escalation. The gap between intention and action is perfectly character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Do you have any hidden inappropriate magazines or videos?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Me? No! Why would I have those? I'm a respectable man. I don't know what you're talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more offended right now?

jokes.text: And X is spelled Mike Hannigan.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just spelled out her name for the charity worker while claiming anonymity.
jokes.punchline: Mike, resigned, gives his actual name as the spelling of 'Mr. X.'
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical button on joke #10. Mike's deadpan resignation to Phoebe's obliviousness is very funny. The phrasing 'X is spelled Mike Hannigan' is an absurdist construction that maximizes the joke in five words.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm just asking where you'd hide something... hypothetically. Like, not in the obvious places—not under the mattress, not in the closet, not behind the books on the shelf. Maybe somewhere like... behind the radiator? Or taped to the back of a drawer? Or inside a hollowed-out book?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, why are you asking me this?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm not! I'm just curious where *you* would hide something.

jokes.text: Oh, look, we get this free T-shirt. Uh, actually that's the shirt I wore to the gym. Um, it's moist.
jokes.setup: Phoebe excitedly grabs what she thinks is a free T-shirt reward for her donation.
jokes.punchline: The charity worker reveals it's his used gym shirt. It's also moist.
jokes.explanation: The word 'moist' as a button is a reliable disgust-comedy tool but deployed well here. The setup (charity reward expectation) subverted by the sweaty reality is funny, and the casual delivery of 'it's moist' earns a bigger reaction than the reveal itself. Rewatch bonus for the visual of Phoebe presumably already holding it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You bought a video?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes, okay? I bought a video. But I want you to know that I bought it for an entirely different reason than you think.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What reason?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I wanted to see what all the fuss was about... for educational purposes!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Educational purposes?!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. Okay, fine. I'm... I'm aware of the issue.

jokes.text: Oh, that's okay. Actually there are tons of other beautiful paleontologists out there. Absolutely. There was one! She's it! All the rest look like they should live under a bridge!
jokes.setup: Rachel offers condolences about Ross's breakup and encourages him by saying there are other beautiful paleontologists.
jokes.punchline: Ross agrees there was exactly one, Charlie, and all other paleontologists are trolls.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalation from 'there are tons of them' to 'there was ONE' to the brutal 'live under a bridge' is perfectly structured and very Ross — his self-pity expressed as scientific taxonomy of paleontologist attractiveness. 'Live under a bridge' is a memorable, specific image. High quotability. Character integration is excellent — only Ross would frame heartbreak through his academic discipline.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I didn't make that video.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, I didn't make it either.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So we're just going to pretend this never happened?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I think that's for the best.

jokes.text: Like I said, I was thinking of taking Emma to the museum of knives and fire.
jokes.setup: Ross says he wants to take Emma to the playground. Rachel reacts with horror.
jokes.punchline: Ross sarcastically 'corrects' his statement to the most dangerous possible destination — a museum of knives and fire — to mock Rachel's overprotective reaction.
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed sarcastic comeback. The 'museum of knives and fire' is a funny specific absurdist invention rather than a generic 'dangerous place.' Economy is high — the joke is delivered in one clean sentence. Quotable.

jokes.text: And it was uneven for weeks.
jokes.setup: Rachel recounts a traumatic childhood swing incident where her hair got tangled and her mom had to cut it.
jokes.punchline: The 'traumatic' climax of the story is that her hair was uneven. For weeks.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The structure is superb: Rachel builds a genuinely traumatic-sounding narrative (trapped hair, emergency cutting) and the audience anticipates real injury — then the devastating punchline is simply uneven hair. 'For weeks' as the final kicker is perfect economy. Deeply character-specific — only vain, appearance-obsessed Rachel would experience lopsided hair as genuine childhood trauma. The pause before delivery (implied by scene beat) makes it land harder. Worthy of an 8+ designation.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I want complete anonymity.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Me too, I don't want anyone to know who I am.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Mike.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm Phoebe Buffay.

jokes.text: And you made it through that?
jokes.setup: Rachel's traumatic swing story culminates in her hair being uneven for weeks.
jokes.punchline: Ross's mock-astonished response treats the uneven hair as though Rachel survived a war.
jokes.explanation: Economical reaction that validates and amplifies the previous joke. The faux-reverence for a trivial complaint is a classic straight-man move executed well. Works in tandem with joke #15.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Recognition isn't necessary.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh good, because we'd like to donate anonymously. That's P-H-O-E-B-E and M-I-K-E.

jokes.text: I wonder who's going to play you in the movie.
jokes.setup: Rachel has described her childhood 'trauma' of uneven hair from a swing accident.
jokes.punchline: Ross implies the story is so dramatic it deserves a movie adaptation — with an actress playing Rachel.
jokes.explanation: Second mock-epic response from Ross, escalating his sarcasm. Works as an escalation of joke #16. The movie-biopic frame is a funny extension of the 'this is a major event' mockery.

jokes.text: And I was thinking Claire Danes.
jokes.setup: Ross wonders who would play Rachel in the movie about her tragic hair trauma. Rachel dismisses him.
jokes.punchline: Ross has already thought about the casting, specifically suggesting Claire Danes.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. The implication that Ross has been genuinely casting the movie biopic of Rachel's hair trauma is very funny. The specific name (Claire Danes) makes it funnier than a generic answer would — it shows Ross committed to the bit. Rewatch bonus because the throwaway specificity rewards attention.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Wow, a free T-shirt! This is amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Charity worker
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's a great shirt. Barely worn.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: This is perfect!

dialogue.speaker: Charity worker
dialogue.line: Well, it's actually my gym shirt. I figured I'd donate it since I upgraded to a new one.

jokes.text: Space is filled with orbiting children.
jokes.setup: Rachel dramatically describes the terror of swings — the moment at the top where you don't know if you'll return to earth.
jokes.punchline: Ross takes her metaphor literally and extends it to absurd sci-fi territory: children becoming orbital objects.
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. Five words of pure absurdist gold. Rachel's overwrought fear of swings reaches a crescendo ('you just don't know if you're going to return back to earth') and Ross's deadpan response takes her metaphor into literal aerospace territory with zero effort. The image of children silently orbiting Earth is genuinely surreal and unexpected. The economy is flawless — no word could be added or removed. Character-specific: Ross is a scientist who would naturally escalate physical fears into planetary mechanics. Highly quotable, completely unpredictable. This is a legitimate 8+ moment by any standard.

dialogue.speaker: Charity worker
dialogue.line: Well, it's not exactly free. It's a used shirt.

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: Used? How used?

dialogue.speaker: Charity worker
dialogue.line: Let's just say the previous owner had a very active lifestyle. Mostly running. From the police.

jokes.text: You don't want to be one of those mothers who pass on their irrational fears to their children, do you? Irrational, huh? Alright, I'll remember that the next time you freak out about a spider in your apartment.
jokes.setup: Ross lectures Rachel about not passing irrational fears to Emma.
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately counters with Ross's own irrational fear of spiders, perfectly deflating his high ground.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom comeback structure — lecturer immediately revealed to be a hypocrite. Well executed but familiar territory. Rachel's response is sharp and comes quickly, which helps.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, you know, there are a lot of talented paleontologists out there doing great work.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: But let's be honest, they're all idiots.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah. That's the same, I'm sure there are 30 different species of poisonous swings.
jokes.setup: Rachel equates Ross's spider fear with her swing fear as equally irrational.
jokes.punchline: Ross invokes his scientific authority to argue the fears are NOT equivalent — there are actual poisonous spiders; there are no poisonous swings.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific joke — Ross's scientist pedantry is the punchline. The sarcastic construct '30 different species of poisonous swings' is a funny specific invention. His instinct to categorize threats taxonomically (species!) is very Ross. Near 8-level craft.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A playground? Ross, that's insane!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, what do you suggest? We could always go bungee jumping off the Brooklyn Bridge instead.

jokes.text: Oh, this is so sweet of you. Oh, but you know what? I won't be needing a veil. I actually won't be wearing a dress at all. I told you I am not coming to a naked wedding!
jokes.setup: Monica gives Phoebe a veil, assuming Phoebe is having a traditional wedding.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe clarifies she won't wear a dress. Monica assumes this means a naked wedding.
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — 'I won't be wearing a dress at all' leads the audience to wonder too, and Monica's pre-established objection to the naked wedding ('I told you') implies this is an ongoing argument. Character-specific for both: Phoebe would seriously consider this, Monica would be genuinely horrified.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I was on this swing, and my hair got caught. It was so traumatic!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, what happened?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: They had to cut it out. I had this huge chunk missing.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That sounds horrible!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It was. But honestly? It was just uneven hair.

jokes.text: Oh, please, I'll put this on and, ugh, I just look like — well, radiant!
jokes.setup: Monica puts on Phoebe's veil, expecting to look ridiculous to reinforce her argument that the veil matters.
jokes.punchline: She looks so good in it that her argument collapses — she can't finish the insult.
jokes.explanation: Visual gag with a good punchline structure. Monica's self-sabotage — trying to prove a point and immediately being undermined by her own vanity — is funny and character-consistent. The rewatch bonus applies because you can see it coming from the moment she puts the veil on.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wow, so you're telling me you survived this traumatic hair experience? That's incredible. I mean, most people don't make it out of a bad haircut alive.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, it's not funny!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, I'm serious. You should write a book. 'I Survived: A Haircut Story.' It'll be huge.

jokes.text: You know, I was just there for jury duty. They've really spruced that place up.
jokes.setup: Phoebe contemplates getting married at city hall as a simple, elegant solution.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's endorsement of city hall is based on her jury duty experience — an entirely unromantic frame of reference.
jokes.explanation: Decent observational humor — the gap between 'romantic city hall wedding' and 'jury duty venue' is funny. 'They've really spruced that place up' is a funny specific detail. Works efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What, you mean like a Lifetime movie? 'Rachel Green: A Story of Survival'? Coming this fall to a cable network near you.

jokes.text: Well, I'll just ask for it back.
jokes.setup: Phoebe realizes she's given all her wedding money to charity and now wants a big wedding.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's solution — simply asking the charity to return the donation — is delivered with complete earnestness.
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe logic — the simplest possible solution delivered without a hint of self-awareness. The character integration is strong; this is exactly how Phoebe's mind works. Sets up the return-the-donation subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, a movie about my trauma? That's actually genius. Who would play me?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It has to be someone who can really capture my vulnerability and... my hair.

jokes.text: That's sweet, honey, but save something for the adoption lady.
jokes.setup: Phoebe declares that her wedding is 'way more important than some stupid kids,' right before Monica and Chandler's adoption interview.
jokes.punchline: Chandler, hearing his future child referred to as a 'stupid kid,' gently asks Phoebe to moderate herself before the social worker arrives.
jokes.explanation: Very sharp timing joke. The irony of Phoebe dismissing 'stupid kids' in front of parents trying desperately to adopt is well-constructed. Chandler's dry response ('save something for the adoption lady') is perfectly economical and very Chandler — managing chaos with resigned wit. High craft.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, so like, when you're on a swing, you have to be SO careful because if you go too high, you literally become a projectile. Like, you could just... fly off into space. And then your hair gets all messed up from the velocity, and you're just floating there in the atmosphere wondering how you're going to get down.

jokes.text: Rach, she's got like three hairs. I know, I know, but they're just so beautiful. Oh my God, I just pulled one out.
jokes.setup: Rachel is terrified about Emma's hair getting caught in the swing chain, the same way hers did.
jokes.punchline: In her anxious hovering, she accidentally pulls out one of Emma's precious few hairs.
jokes.explanation: Well-structured callback to the hair trauma storyline. The irony is that Rachel's protective hovering causes the exact kind of hair incident she fears. 'Three hairs' is a specific, funny detail. The escalation from obsessing over three hairs to immediately pulling one out is perfectly timed.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, so if I swing any higher, what happens?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, at a certain point, you achieve escape velocity and just... drift into space.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's not funny!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Actually, it kind of is.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And then you become a new planet. 'Planet Rachel.' Very exclusive real estate.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Technically speaking, you'd need significantly more mass to—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, not now!

jokes.text: Alright, now. Is this guy gay or straight? Because one of us is going to have to start flirting. Gay, go!
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Mike return to the charity to try to get their donation back.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's strategy for getting the money back is for one of them to flirt with the clerk — and she immediately assigns Mike based on a split-second gay/straight assessment.
jokes.explanation: Fast-moving, well-structured joke. The tactical assessment ('one of us is going to have to start flirting') is funny on its own, but the immediate 'Gay, go!' command to Mike is the real laugh — Phoebe as a general deploying her husband into romantic combat. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A swing is not a bug, Ross!

jokes.text: Oh my God! I love your shirt.
jokes.setup: Phoebe commands Mike to flirt with the (apparently gay) charity clerk.
jokes.punchline: Mike's opening flirtation gambit is a compliment on the clerk's shirt — hilariously awkward and stilted.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. Mike's desperate, clearly-not-a-natural flirtation opener is funny precisely because it's the most generic compliment possible. The enthusiastic delivery of a terrible line is relatable and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: They're here! They're here!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, okay. Just be yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I am myself.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know, that's what I'm afraid of.

dialogue.speaker: Visitor
dialogue.line: Hi, we're looking for Creepy?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Creepy?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, they think our apartment number is a name!

jokes.text: Yeah. This feels really good.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just been told she's asking children's charity to refund a donation.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe, oblivious to the moral irony, says this feels really good — echoing her earlier statement when she made the donation.
jokes.explanation: Economical callback that earns its laugh through irony. Phoebe said 'it feels so good' when donating; now she says the same thing about taking the money back from children. The self-unawareness is perfectly Phoebe and the callback is well-timed. Rewatch bonus for catching the symmetry.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm not wearing a dress.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Dresses are a tool of the patriarchy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's my wedding!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know, and it's going to be beautiful. I'm just gonna wear pants.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, are we having a lesbian wedding?

jokes.text: Besides, this is probably a good thing. We've really been spoiling the children with all the food and warm clothing.
jokes.setup: The charity worker reluctantly accepts that Phoebe and Mike want their money back.
jokes.punchline: He sarcastically suggests that depriving children of food and clothing is actually beneficial — they've been getting too much.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely dark and funny. The deadpan delivery of 'spoiling the children with food and warm clothing' is the kind of dark wit that elevates a sitcom above average. The specific items — food and warm clothing, the most basic needs — make the cruelty of the joke land harder. High impact.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I don't care about looking nice for the wedding. It's not important to me.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God! I look like a princess! I'm so beautiful!

jokes.text: I didn't have a graduation party and I didn't go to prom. And I spent my sweet 16 being chased around a tire yard by an escaped mental patient who, in his own words, 'wanted to kill me' or whatever.
jokes.setup: Phoebe passionately argues that she deserves a real wedding because she missed out on other life milestones.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from missed graduation to missed prom arrives at 'being chased by an escaped mental patient at my sweet sixteen' — the 'or whatever' at the end is the perfect button.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top two jokes. The escalation structure is excellent — two relatable missed milestones (graduation, prom) followed by an absurdly horrific one (attempted murder at sweet sixteen). The specificity of 'tire yard' and 'in his own words' elevates it from a generic dark joke to something vividly imagined. The 'or whatever' as a dismissive button after 'wanted to kill me' is a brilliant choice — Phoebe treats near-death as an afterthought while fighting for her wedding. Perfectly integrates Phoebe's established backstory of a traumatic childhood. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know, city hall marriages are very romantic. I mean, look at jury duty - people meet, they fall in love, they make a lifetime commitment.

jokes.text: She could've been talking about either one of us.
jokes.setup: Phoebe calls the charity worker a 'sweaty little man' as she storms off.
jokes.punchline: Mike notes the description fits both him and the charity worker, delivered with complete calm.
jokes.explanation: Clean, economic button. Mike's self-deprecating observation delivered with zero drama is very funny. The joke works because it comes from a character who is meant to be suave — his willingness to include himself as a possible 'sweaty little man' is disarming.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We're taking the money back from the children's hospital? What if a child needs a... a new liver?

jokes.text: Because we love kids. Love 'em to death. Well, not actually to death. That's just a figure of speech. We love kids the appropriate amount. As allowed by law.
jokes.setup: Chandler enthusiastically tells the adoption social worker they love kids, trying to make a good impression.
jokes.punchline: He over-corrects 'love 'em to death' into an increasingly alarming series of disclaimers that make everything worse.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and very high craft. The escalating self-correction is a classic Chandler set piece. Each correction digs him deeper: 'not to death' → 'just a figure of speech' → 'the appropriate amount' → 'as allowed by law.' The final phrase 'as allowed by law' is a perfect absurdist button that implies familiarity with legal limits on child affection. Deeply character-specific — Chandler's anxiety manifesting as verbal spiraling in the worst possible moment. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could you BE any more hostile toward children?

jokes.text: We love kids the appropriate amount. As allowed by law.
jokes.setup: Chandler has just over-corrected about loving kids 'to death.'
jokes.punchline: His attempt to sound measured and safe instead produces the creepy legalese 'as allowed by law' — which implies the law needs to cap how much you can love children.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'As allowed by law' is an astonishing escalation — in trying to sound safe and measured, Chandler accidentally implies that loving children too much requires legal regulation. The escalation from 'to death' → 'appropriate amount' → 'as allowed by law' is a three-beat structure where each beat is worse than the last. Highly quotable, perfectly Chandler, and would get one of the biggest laughs of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, her hair! Be careful with her hair!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, she's three years old. She has like five hairs.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Exactly! Five hairs! And I am not losing a single one!

jokes.text: Is that that couple on the first floor? Because we should get a baby before them! That guy tried to sell me drugs!
jokes.setup: The social worker mentions she feels she's been to the building before, wondering if other couples are adopting.
jokes.punchline: Chandler panics and immediately attacks the competition (a drug dealer on the first floor), framing it as why they deserve the baby more.
jokes.explanation: Good Chandler panic joke — the competitive desperation of adoption-list positioning collides with the revelation that his neighbor is a drug dealer. The specificity ('that guy tried to sell me drugs') is funny and the competitive framing ('we should get a baby before them') is appropriately absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Emma's hair is so delicate. I have to be so careful.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: One wrong move and it could all fall out.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm just going to gently...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh no! No no no no no!

jokes.text: But other than that, wholesome, wholesome building.
jokes.setup: Chandler has just revealed that a neighbor tried to sell him drugs, undermining his claim that the building has a 'wholesome family feel.'
jokes.punchline: He doubles down on 'wholesome' anyway, as if the drug dealer is a minor footnote.
jokes.explanation: Solid button on the previous joke. The repetition of 'wholesome' twice is funny — it's too emphatic, betraying Chandler's desperation. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me you want your donation back?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes, we need it for something else.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: So... you're taking money away from children with cancer.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: When you say it like that, it sounds bad.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I'm not a bad guy, but right now, I'm definitely looking like one.

jokes.text: Ugh, that wouldn't by any chance be Joey Tribbiani. Oh, yes! Of course it was.
jokes.setup: The social worker reveals she went on a bad date with someone in the building who never called her back.
jokes.punchline: Before she can say the name, Chandler guesses immediately — because of course it's Joey. Monica confirms with resigned exasperation.
jokes.explanation: Good running-character joke — Joey's reputation for not calling women back is so well established that Chandler can identify him as the culprit with zero information. The resigned 'Of course it was' from Monica is a perfect button. The impending disaster for their adoption interview is well set-up here.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, so we need to charm her. I'll use my wiles.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Your wiles?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm very wily. I once convinced a man to give me his car.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: How?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I told him it was a really nice car.

jokes.text: So you're not friends with him? Oh, God, no! No, no, no, no. No! Nope...... No, no, no, no....
jokes.setup: The social worker asks if Monica and Chandler are friends with Joey — who is their best friend.
jokes.punchline: Monica (and presumably Chandler) emphatically deny any friendship with Joey in an increasingly desperate cascade of 'no's.
jokes.explanation: Cringe comedy done well. The escalating denial ('No! Nope...... No, no, no, no') is funny because the audience knows Joey lives literally next door and is their best friend. The extended pause implied by the ellipsis before resuming denial suggests Monica's internal spiral. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, I'll do it. I'll flirt with him.

jokes.text: Hello. Anybody in there ordered a celebrity? Ow! What was that? Oh, that's just some crazy guy who roams the halls here. He's great with kids though.
jokes.setup: Joey knocks on the door to offer his celebrity help during the adoption interview — right after Monica and Chandler denied knowing him.
jokes.punchline: Monica physically stops Joey from entering (the 'Ow!'). They cover by calling him a 'crazy guy who roams the halls.' Chandler adds he's 'great with kids' as a tonal non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe comedy escalation. 'Anybody in there ordered a celebrity?' is a funny Joey line — he thinks this is a casual drop-in. The physical comedy (someone hitting him through the door, inferred from 'Ow!') and the cover story of 'crazy hall roamer' is well-executed sitcom farce. 'He's great with kids though' is a nice absurd button from Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Hey... do you come here often?

dialogue.speaker: Charity Worker
dialogue.line: It's a charity event. I work here.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Right, right. So... you ever think about... not working here?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Mike, stop.

jokes.text: Oh, relax! I didn't say the F word.
jokes.setup: Ross gets hurt at the playground and yells 'Son of a bitch!' in front of Rachel.
jokes.punchline: He defends himself by clarifying he didn't say the actual F-word — as if 'son of a bitch' is perfectly acceptable.
jokes.explanation: Quick, clean joke. The logic of 'that was fine because I didn't say THE word' while having clearly said something equally inappropriate is funny in its specificity. Economy is high. Familiar sitcom territory but executed efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, it feels great to give to charity. It really warms your heart. Of course, it also empties your wallet, but that's a small price to pay for feeling morally superior to everyone around you.

jokes.text: Ross, see, I told you the swings are evil!
jokes.setup: Ross has just been injured by the playground swing.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's earlier paranoid fear of swings is now 'vindicated' — even though the injury was caused by adult clumsiness, not swing malevolence.
jokes.explanation: Good callback that uses the physical comedy payoff to validate Rachel's earlier irrational fear. The fact that the swing injured Ross (not Emma) makes it funnier — the fear is still irrational but Rachel refuses to acknowledge the distinction.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We'd like our donation back.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Yeah, we need it.

dialogue.speaker: Charity worker
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, but once a donation is made, we can't return it.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, that's not very charitable of you.

dialogue.speaker: Charity worker
dialogue.line: The money goes directly to helping children in need - food, shelter, education.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, you're spoiling them.

jokes.text: I know what this is all about. You've always been jealous of my hair.
jokes.setup: Ross tries to get Rachel to get on the swing to prove it's safe.
jokes.punchline: Rachel deflects by accusing Ross of a hidden motive — hair jealousy — an absurd psychological projection.
jokes.explanation: Fun character-specific absurdism. Rachel's narcissistic framing — that Ross's concern for her fear is secretly about jealousy of her superior hair — is very consistent with her vanity. The callback to the hair theme ties it together nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I want a real wedding! I want a dress and a cake and flowers and a real honeymoon! I didn't have a real birthday party until I was in my twenties because my mother was in jail.

jokes.text: Alright, fine! I'll do it! Good. If you hold the spider. What? Where? Where? 'IF' you hold a spider. I know.
jokes.setup: Ross pressures Rachel to get on the swing to face her fear. She agrees — with a condition.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's condition is that Ross hold a spider (his own irrational fear). Ross panics immediately at the mention of spider, then embarrassedly admits he knew it was hypothetical.
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed callback payoff. The parallel fears are finally deployed against each other. Ross's immediate 'What? Where? Where?' panic reaction to the word 'spider' is excellent physical/verbal comedy, and his sheepish 'I know' after Rachel clarifies it was hypothetical is a perfect button showing his self-awareness about the absurdity. High character integration for both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You're a sweaty little man!

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Hey, that's not fair. I'm not sweaty.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You are too!

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Well, yeah, okay, I'm a little sweaty. But so is that charity guy over there.

jokes.text: What's going on? Oh, just like I said, that crazy... Bert roaming the halls. Guys. Keep on roaming, Bert! We don't want any crazy today!
jokes.setup: Joey returns to the apartment door again, forcing Monica and Chandler to maintain the 'crazy hall guy named Bert' cover story.
jokes.punchline: Monica commands Joey to 'keep roaming' and they 'don't want any crazy today' — speaking to their best friend as if he's a stranger.
jokes.explanation: Running gag execution — the Bert cover story returning and Monica having to shout 'keep on roaming' to Joey is a solid cringe beat. Loses some novelty as a repeat but the escalation of Monica playing along so enthusiastically is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're very excited about having a black baby.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: An African American baby. Oh God, I'm gonna say something wrong, aren't I?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, no, you're doing great.

jokes.text: Is he alright out there by himself? Oh, yeah. He has a caretaker, his older brother. Ernie.
jokes.setup: The social worker is concerned about the apparently mentally unstable 'Bert' roaming the halls alone.
jokes.punchline: Chandler improvises that Bert has a caretaker — his older brother Ernie — a Sesame Street reference that arrives with a perfect straight face.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever joke. Chandler improvising 'Bert' as the cover name (accidentally or not) and then being forced to extend the Sesame Street metaphor by adding 'Ernie' as the caretaker is a great escalation. The timing and deadpan delivery are essential. Rewatch bonus for the implicit realization that 'Bert' was the code word AND a Sesame Street character, and Chandler committed to the bit perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I love kids.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, that came out a little wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, I love kids. I want to have kids.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's not better.

jokes.text: Bert and Ernie? You can't make this stuff up!
jokes.setup: Chandler has just named the imaginary hall-roamer 'Bert' with caretaker brother 'Ernie.'
jokes.punchline: The social worker's delighted reaction — 'You can't make this stuff up!' — is itself the joke, because they absolutely did make it up.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Bert/Ernie joke. The irony of 'you can't make this stuff up' in a situation where it was entirely made up is a clean meta-joke. The social worker's credulity makes the deception funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Social Worker
dialogue.line: Have you considered that other couples might be adopting too?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? No! We're getting those babies!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And I don't appreciate you trying to make us compete with some couple from... from New Jersey or something!

jokes.text: Oh, it ended okay. One of my friends shot him.
jokes.setup: Mike sympathizes about Phoebe's sweet-sixteen tire yard trauma with the escaped mental patient.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe casually mentions the resolution was that someone shot the mental patient — delivered as a cheerful resolution.
jokes.explanation: Superb dark comedy button on the earlier sweet-sixteen joke. Phoebe's matter-of-fact cheerfulness about a friend shooting someone is pitch-perfect character comedy — she's been through so much that this barely registers as notable. 'It ended okay' as a preface to 'one of my friends shot him' is an excellent structure. The economy is excellent at eight words for the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I just accused our neighbor of drug dealing! What if he sues us? What if the building gets condemned? What if nobody wants to live here anymore?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, relax. I'm sure it's fine.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Fine?! Chandler, we live in a building where people think there are drugs! We might as well be living in a crack house!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, what's wrong with that? I lived in a crack house once.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's not helping, Joey!

jokes.text: And if that guy at the charity gives us a hard time, my friend hasn't shot anyone in a really long time.
jokes.setup: Mike agrees to give the wedding money back to charity. Phoebe worries the charity worker will be difficult.
jokes.punchline: Mike casually references using Phoebe's friend (the shooter from joke #48) as leverage — implying violence if necessary.
jokes.explanation: Good callback that extends the dark joke. 'Hasn't shot anyone in a really long time' implies the friend is overdue, which is a funny dark construction. Mike's growing comfort with Phoebe's chaotic world is shown through his easy deployment of this threat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You didn't call the social worker back? What is wrong with you? Oh, that's right, everything.

jokes.text: Oh, by the way, you're more than welcome to look under any of the furniture because, believe me, you won't find any porn or cigarettes under there.
jokes.setup: The social worker compliments the apartment environment. Chandler, still anxious, tries to be helpful.
jokes.punchline: He volunteers the information that there's no porn or cigarettes under the furniture — a confession framed as an invitation, drawing attention to the exact things that were there.
jokes.explanation: Strong callback payoff. The anxiety-driven Freudian slip of inviting the social worker to search for the exact contraband that was just removed is very Chandler — his nervousness causing him to torpedo himself. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Friends with Joey? No, no, no. We're not... I mean, we barely know each other. He's just someone who lives here. I don't even like him that much, honestly. And he definitely doesn't like me. We have nothing in common. Nothing! We don't hang out, we don't talk, we don't... Why are you looking at me like that? Fine! Yes, okay, we're friends with Joey!

jokes.text: Well, you wouldn't let me in so I thought you were in trouble! But you called me Bert! That's our code word for danger! We don't have a code word! We don't?
jokes.setup: Joey breaks in thinking they're in danger because they called him 'Bert.'
jokes.punchline: Joey has assigned 'Bert' as a secret code word for danger without telling anyone — and then is genuinely surprised to learn they don't have a code word.
jokes.explanation: Very funny Joey moment — his self-assigned secret code word that he never shared with anyone is very Joey. The genuine surprise at 'We don't have a code word? We don't?' shows his obliviousness without malice. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Joey Tribbiani. You may know me from such films as... well, actually, you probably don't know me from any films. But I'm an actor! And I'm very talented. And I'm very, very good-looking.

jokes.text: From now on, Bert will be our code word for danger. So that was the baby's room.
jokes.setup: Joey has burst in through the window/wall and chaos has ensued during the adoption interview.
jokes.punchline: Chandler matter-of-factly adopts the code word mid-crisis, then Monica immediately pivots back to the tour of the apartment as if nothing happened.
jokes.explanation: Good beat — Monica's ability to snap back to hostess mode with 'So that was the baby's room' after complete chaos is very Monica. Chandler's resignation to accepting the code word mid-crisis is very Chandler. The pivot is fast and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He's great with kids!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: He's a little crazy, but he's great with kids.

jokes.text: Ah, what room should we see next? Any room that isn't behind this couch.
jokes.setup: Monica tries to continue the apartment tour after Joey has apparently hidden behind the couch.
jokes.punchline: The social worker asks which room to see next. Monica's answer is to steer away from wherever Joey is hiding.
jokes.explanation: Clean cringe joke — Monica accidentally reveals Joey's hiding spot by telling the social worker not to look there. The specificity ('behind this couch') makes it funnier than a vague deflection would be.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Son of a bitch!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross! The baby!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? I didn't say the F-word!

jokes.text: Some people don't get him but I think he's really funny.
jokes.setup: The social worker has just witnessed Joey crash through the apartment and hide behind the couch.
jokes.punchline: Chandler defends the 'crazy roaming Bert' as genuinely funny, breaking character in a moment of honest appreciation for Joey.
jokes.explanation: Lovely character moment disguised as a joke. Chandler's affection for Joey breaking through his panic — 'Some people don't get him but I think he's really funny' — is both funny and genuinely sweet. The understatement of defending a chaos agent as 'funny' while in an adoption interview is very Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Come on, try the swing. It'll be fun!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, so you want me to go on the swing so you can watch me and think about how pretty I look while I'm swinging?

jokes.text: What? I forgot my bat.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler have frantically gotten Joey out of the apartment. He immediately returns.
jokes.punchline: His reason for returning: he forgot his bat. No explanation of why he had a bat or what it's for.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. The bat is introduced with zero context and never explained — why Joey has a baseball bat at a neighborly visit is a mystery that makes it funnier. The economy is nearly perfect: two words for a massive laugh. The bat will also recur as a callback, adding rewatch bonus. Pure absurdist Joey comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, okay. I'll try the swing if you hold a spider.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A spider?! No, no, no. Absolutely not. I can't do that.

jokes.text: And for the last time, we do not want to be friends with you! And we don't want to buy your bat!
jokes.setup: Monica is furiously trying to get Joey out of the apartment a third time.
jokes.punchline: In her desperation she preemptively rejects buying his bat — confirming Joey was apparently trying to sell it, raising more questions than it answers.
jokes.explanation: Good dual callback — Monica denying friendship AND rejecting a bat purchase simultaneously is a funny escalation. The implication that Joey offered to sell the bat to his best friends in the middle of their adoption interview is wonderfully Joey. The bat plot thickens without explanation.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A-DOP-SHUN!

jokes.text: What's going on? Bert, Bert, Bert.
jokes.setup: The social worker hears the commotion and comes to see what's happening.
jokes.punchline: Chandler uses 'Bert' as an incantation — repeating it three times to invoke the code word for danger — which now means nothing to anyone present except Joey.
jokes.explanation: Running gag maintenance. Chandler invoking 'Bert, Bert, Bert' as his only tool is funny in its desperation. Loses some impact as a third iteration of the same gag but the triple repetition adds an incantation quality that's funny.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Who's Bert?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: The crazy guy in the hall!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, him. Yeah, he's not really our friend.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah. You have got some nerve coming back here. I can't believe you never called me!
jokes.setup: The social worker confronts Joey, apparently ready to be angry at him for the disruption.
jokes.punchline: Instead of being angry about the apartment invasion, the social worker's grievance is that Joey never called her — she's still wounded by the date.
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection payoff — the audience expects professional anger, gets personal romantic grievance. The pivot to 'I can't believe you never called me' is well-timed and uses the established backstory well.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey needs supervision.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're calling him Ernie.

jokes.text: No, no, you know, too late for apologies, okay? You broke my heart. You know how many women I had to sleep with to get over you?
jokes.setup: The social worker apologizes. Joey, now playing the wounded party, refuses to let it go.
jokes.punchline: Joey frames sleeping with many women as a form of heartbreak recovery — revealing that his 'getting over her' involved mass dating, which is both funny and completely Joey.
jokes.explanation: Very strong joke. 'You know how many women I had to sleep with to get over you?' is funny as a romantic grievance and also as an inadvertent confession. The framing of womanizing as a coping mechanism for heartbreak is very Joey — his logic is internally consistent even when absurd. High character integration and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Bert and Ernie? No, no, no. It's Gellir and Bing.

dialogue.speaker: Social Worker
dialogue.line: Those aren't real names.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, we're not making them up!

jokes.text: Boy, you people are nice. And I've got to say, I think you're going to make excellent parents.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler apologize for the chaos of Joey's intrusion.
jokes.punchline: The social worker, far from being alienated, declares them excellent parent candidates — the entire Joey disaster has somehow helped their case.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the entire adoption interview subplot. The irony that the chaotic Joey situation — which Monica and Chandler feared would destroy their chances — actually charmed the social worker is a satisfying ironic reversal. The warmth of the moment is genuine, adding to the impact.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: My Sweet 16 was terrible. My friend shot a mental patient.

jokes.text: Boy, you people are nice. And I've got to say, I think you're going to make excellent parents.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler watch helplessly as Joey melodramatically confronts the social worker about their lost date — a completely embarrassing situation during an adoption interview.
jokes.punchline: The social worker concludes from this chaos that Monica and Chandler will make excellent parents — a completely unexpected positive outcome from a disaster.
jokes.explanation: Good subversion — the entire Joey subplot has been building toward disaster, and the payoff is that it somehow HELPS. The social worker's reasoning ('you people are nice') is the ironic twist. This is an earned comedic reversal that also advances the plot.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, so he's ready to shoot again?

jokes.text: Boy, you people are nice. And I've got to say, I think you're going to make excellent parents.
jokes.setup: The adoption interview has been a complete disaster — hidden contraband, a 'crazy hall roamer,' Joey's chaotic presence, Chandler's anxiety-fueled verbal disasters.
jokes.punchline: Despite all of it, the social worker concludes they'll make excellent parents — with 'boy, you people are nice' as a genuine assessment.
jokes.explanation: The punchline to the entire adoption interview subplot. After everything, the social worker's conclusion is positive — but 'you people are nice' as the reason suggests she's judging them on personality rather than the chaotic evidence of the visit. It's a satisfying structural payoff while also being slightly absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Everything is clean. Spotless. I even organized the cabinets by color and food group.

dialogue.speaker: Social Worker
dialogue.line: That's... very thorough.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And I want you to know, there are absolutely no dead bodies in the freezer.

dialogue.speaker: Social Worker
dialogue.line: ...I wasn't going to check.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Or in the walls. The walls are clean too.

jokes.text: Oh, if I haven't said so already, sir, congratulations.
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Mike return to the charity for the second time in one day, this time to give the money back.
jokes.punchline: The charity worker congratulates one of them — presumably Mike — for enduring Phoebe, in a tone that implies he's been watching the whole circus.
jokes.explanation: Good understated joke from the charity worker character. 'Congratulations, sir' — presumably for being engaged to Phoebe — is a funny note of sympathy that works as a good button on the charity subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, we don't have a code word?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We need a code word!

jokes.text: Okay, look, enough! Alright? I'm stepping in and I put my foot down. As your future husband, I'm going to make this decision for us. No, what do you think we should do?
jokes.setup: Mike announces he's taking charge and making the decision for both of them.
jokes.punchline: He immediately asks Phoebe what she thinks they should do — completely undermining his declaration of authority.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom husband-caves-immediately joke, but executed with good pacing. The build-up of authority ('I'm stepping in,' 'I put my foot down,' 'as your future husband') followed by immediate capitulation makes the punchline land with appropriate absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We need a code word. Something we can say if things get really bad during the birth.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't know. Something that means 'I can't take it anymore, get me drugs.'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How about 'Bert'?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Bert? Why Bert?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't know, it just came to me.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. Bert it is.

jokes.text: On behalf of the children of New York, I reject your money. But we're giving you this. And I'm giving it back to you. Come on. Consider it a contribution.
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Mike try to give the money back to charity. The charity worker refuses to take it back.
jokes.punchline: The charity worker rejects the donation — now refusing to take money that was originally refused as a refund. The check changes hands multiple times in an absurd loop.
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist payoff to the charitable giving plot. The check ping-ponging back and forth is a funny visual loop, and 'On behalf of the children of New York, I reject your money' is a funny formal declaration. The resolution is generous and character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, he's a complex character. Very physical. Sometimes he says things that don't quite make sense, but the audience seems to love him anyway. He's not the brightest, but he has a certain charm. And frankly, the show wouldn't work without him.

jokes.text: And when you do, make sure you ask for Brian. Oh, is that you? No.
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Mike agree to come back in a few years to make a bigger donation. The charity worker invites them to ask for him.
jokes.punchline: He isn't Brian. He just directed them to ask for someone else.
jokes.explanation: Clean, economical joke. The charity worker's self-deprecating redirect implies he won't be there in a few years, or he simply isn't the person best suited for major donations. The flat 'No' is a funny button. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait! I forgot my... my... lucky adoption interviewing tie!

jokes.text: Hello. Have you seen Joey's bat?
jokes.setup: The episode appears to be wrapping up. Joey shows up at Monica and Chandler's door.
jokes.punchline: His only mission: to locate his bat. The bat returns as the final punchline of the episode's B-plot.
jokes.explanation: Perfect tag scene joke. The bat, introduced as an absurdist non-sequitur, never explained, supposedly being sold to Monica and Chandler, now gets a final callback as the last moment of the Joey subplot. 'Have you seen Joey's bat?' with zero other context is the ideal button — it completes the bat's arc (still missing, still unexplained) and rewards viewers who've been tracking the gag. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I got a bat.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You're selling it?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, I'm keeping it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Then why are you telling me?

jokes.text: Okay. I got a spider. There were two. I picked the bigger one.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel's mutual-fear face-off — she gets on the swing if he holds a spider.
jokes.punchline: Rachel has actually caught a spider. And she upgraded to the bigger one, treating this like a tactical mission.
jokes.explanation: Strong tag scene callback. 'There were two. I picked the bigger one' shows Rachel's competitive character applied to the irrational fear standoff — she went all-in. This is very Rachel: if she's going to do something, she's going to win at it. Good character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Bert! Bert! BERT!

jokes.text: You know what? I'm actually getting used to this little guy. I don't really even feel him in here any more. That's because it's on your neck. What? Ross!
jokes.setup: Ross holds the spider and talks himself into feeling comfortable with it.
jokes.punchline: He can't feel it because it has crawled onto his neck — revealed just as his confidence peaks.
jokes.explanation: Strong physical comedy button to close the episode. The structure is very good — Ross's confident 'I don't even feel him anymore' is the perfect setup for the spider having escaped his hand. 'That's because it's on your neck' is a clean revelation. The rewatch bonus applies because you can anticipate it once Rachel's face reacts before the line. Good final button for the fear subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Of course I remember your name!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's... Lady.

tmdb_overview: Monica and Chandler nervously prepare for a visit from an adoption worker who will decide if they would be suitable parents. Meanwhile, Phoebe and Mike keep changing their minds about donating their wedding money to a children's charity. And Ross tries to help Rachel overcome her fear of swing sets so that baby Emma can enjoy the playground.
insight: Final season adoption episode leans on character comfort over fresh material.
